title: Swimming Eases Chronic Low Back Pain, Landmark Australian Study Finds
excerpt: An eight-week swimming program cut disability by 50% in participants with chronic back pain, according to the first randomized controlled trial of its kind published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine.
body:
• An eight-week swimming program reduced disability by 50% in chronic back pain patients.
  • Swimmers scored 30% lower on a disability scale compared to those receiving education alone.
  • The benefits of swimming persisted at six-month and one-year follow-ups, although the differences narrowed.
  • The EduSwim trial is the first randomized controlled trial to provide clinical evidence supporting swimming as an effective treatment for chronic low back pain.

First Clinical Evidence for Swimming

Swimming has long been recommended by doctors as a low-impact exercise for people with back pain, but until now, no rigorous clinical trial had tested whether it actually works. A landmark study from Australia's Macquarie University has changed that.

Published on July 21 in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, the EduSwim trial is the first randomized controlled trial to show that an individualized swimming program can significantly reduce disability from chronic low back pain — defined as pain lasting 12 weeks or longer.

"Swimming is commonly recommended as an exercise for people with chronic low back pain, but there was a complete lack of evidence about whether it actually works."

— Deborah Wareham, Lead Researcher, Macquarie University

How the Study Worked

Researchers recruited 76 adults aged 26 to 74 — with an average age of 41 — who had experienced some disability due to low back pain for at least 12 weeks. Participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups.

The intervention group received an eight-week individualized swimming program tailored to each participant's ability and fitness, complemented by education about back pain and supported by four telehealth coaching sessions with a physiotherapist. The goal was to build up to three sessions of 30 to 45 minutes per week by the end of the program. Participants were not regular swimmers but could swim 25 meters confidently.

The control group received one to two physiotherapy sessions covering the same educational messages — including that "pain does not always equal harm" and "the back is made for movement" — but otherwise continued their usual treatment.

Significant Improvements

After eight weeks, the swimming group saw striking results. Participants improved by about 50% from their baseline disability levels, according to lead researcher Deborah Wareham, a physiotherapist and PhD candidate in the Spinal Pain Research Centre at Macquarie University.

"Compared to the control group who received education only, swimmers scored on average 2.5 points or 30% lower on a widely used disability scale," Wareham told News-Medical.

Secondary outcomes including pain intensity, functional limitation, and fear of movement also improved more in the swimming group. The benefits persisted at 26-week and 52-week follow-ups, though the difference between groups narrowed over time as some participants stopped swimming — potentially due to lack of enjoyment or limited pool access, according to The Sun.

Why Swimming Works

The researchers say water's natural buoyancy is key to swimming's therapeutic value. It allows people to engage with movements that might otherwise be painful or impossible on land.

"Swimming can improve range of motion, strength and general aerobic capacity and the buoyancy of water can help people engage with movements that might otherwise be painful or limited."

— Professor Mark Hancock, Co-Director, Spinal Pain Research Centre

The results compare favorably with Pilates, one of the few exercises previously shown to help chronic back pain in clinical trials. Wareham noted the improvement was on par with effects reported in a recent meta-analysis of Pilates for back pain.

A related crossover study by the same Macquarie University team, published earlier in Annals of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine, found that backstroke produced less pain than breaststroke during swimming sessions, suggesting that stroke selection may also matter for back pain management.

Relevance for the Indian Diaspora

Low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide, and India carries one of the largest burdens globally. For Indians abroad — many working long hours at desks in technology, healthcare, and finance — chronic back pain is a widespread concern. Community pools across the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia offer accessible starting points for those looking to try swimming as a treatment option, though researchers stress that a physiotherapist's guidance helps tailor the program for best results.

What's Next

The researchers say swimming should now be recommended alongside Pilates and other evidence-based exercises for chronic back pain. Professor Hancock noted that many participants used swimming as a gateway to other physical activities, building confidence to re-engage with exercise more broadly.

"Now we have the evidence to support the recommendation — swimming is a suitable exercise for people with back pain, and it helps," Hancock said.
